edges.description: Surface corynebacteria synthesize porphyrins within the infected horny layer.
The chronic superficial infection produces intertriginous discoloration and scale.
Porphyrin fluorescence marks erythrasma-affected skin under Wood lamp illumination.
Fine scaling is part of the visible intertriginous lesion.
Brown hyperpigmentation or other darker color change can accompany erythrasma patches.
Redness of the infected fold is part of the visible lesion.
Lesions often show a hypopigmented centre within a hyperpigmented scaling rim.
Diabetes is associated with a higher frequency of erythrasma; the cited sources report the association without establishing how it favours corynebacterial overgrowth.

nodes.description: Erythrasma produces erythema, scaling, and skin discoloration in the infected folds; redness can appear as darker or violaceous color change in darker skin.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma: a systematic review of interventions.
evidence.snippet: Cutaneous features include erythema, scaling and skin discoloration; notably, erythema may not manifest as classic redness in individuals with darker skin tones, instead appearing as subtle darkening, violaceous, or other colour changes.

nodes.description: Coral-pink fluorescence under a Wood lamp helps distinguish erythrasma from clinically similar fungal or noninfectious intertriginous dermatoses.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Differential diagnoses of candidiasis, dermatophyte infection, erythrasma, pityriasis versicolor, and terra firma-forme dermatosis were considered. Wood lamp examination revealed bright coral-pink fluorescence. Correlation of the clinical examination and the Wood lamp finding established the diagnosis of erythrasma.

nodes.description: C. minutissimum produces coproporphyrin III and other porphyrins in the superficial infected skin, generating coral-pink fluorescence during Wood lamp examination.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of erythrasma can be confirmed through observing coral-pink fluorescence during Wood lamp examination of the affected skin. Porphyrins, predominantly coproporphyrin III, made by Corynebacteria are the origin of this distinguishing fluorescence.

nodes.description: Erythrasma is more common in people with diabetes mellitus, especially as interdigital toe-web infection.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: It is more commonly found in diabetic and elderly populations. Indeed, erythrasma makes up 17.6% of bacterial skin infections in the elderly and 44% of toe web infections in individuals with diabetes

evidence.snippet: Erythrasma is a chronic superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, predominantly affecting intertriginous areas.

nodes.description: Oral macrolides such as clarithromycin or erythromycin inhibit bacterial ribosomal protein synthesis and provide systemic antibiotic alternatives for erythrasma when topical therapy is impractical or insufficient.

evidence.reference_title: A comparison between the effectiveness of erythromycin, single-dose clarithromycin and topical fusidic acid in the treatment of erythrasma.
evidence.snippet: When the efficacy of clarithromycin and erythromycin therapy was compared, clarithromycin therapy was significantly more effective than erythromycin therapy at 48 h.

evidence.reference_title: Management of cutaneous erythrasma.
evidence.snippet: Erythromycin 250mg four times daily for 14 days is the treatment of choice and other antibacterials include tetracycline and chloramphenicol;

nodes.description: Topical agents, including fusidic acid, clindamycin, mupirocin and the azole clotrimazole, treat erythrasma by suppressing C. minutissimum in the superficial stratum corneum while limiting systemic adverse effects.

evidence.reference_title: A comparison between the effectiveness of erythromycin, single-dose clarithromycin and topical fusidic acid in the treatment of erythrasma.
evidence.snippet: According to the mean of Wood's light reflection scores, the efficacy of fusidic acid cream therapy was significantly higher than other therapies.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma: a systematic review of interventions.
evidence.snippet: A comprehensive review of studies published between 1971 and 2024, including randomized controlled trials and comparative clinical studies, revealed that both clotrimazole and fusidic acid are effective topical options, with fusidic acid providing faster symptom relief, greater reduction in Wood's lamp fluorescence and fewer side-effects.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Topical treatment options for erythrasma include clindamycin, fusidic acid, mupirocin

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Clindamycin is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, disrupting protein synthesis. The topical application of this agent three times per day for one week can lead to complete eradication of erythrasma with no recurrence.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The patient's skin infection was successfully treated with twice daily topical application of 2% mupirocin ointment for six weeks.

evidence.reference_title: Erythrasma Revisited: Diagnosis, Differential Diagnoses, and Comprehensive Review of Treatment.
evidence.snippet: This pathogen infects the stratum corneum in warm and wet areas of the skin. Most commonly, the axillary, inguinal, and interdigital regions are affected.

evidence.reference_title: Management of cutaneous erythrasma.
evidence.snippet: It is found mostly in occluded intertriginous areas such as the axillae, inframammary areas, interspaces of the toes, intergluteal and crural folds, and is more common in individuals with diabetes mellitus than other clinical patients.
